name: Antidisestablishmentarianism
summary: Opposition to removing the Church of England's established status, meaning its legal tie to the Crown, Parliament and state ceremony. Defenders argue that establishment gives every English person access to the church's rites, tempers religious and nationalist extremism, and keeps religion tied to the common life of the nation.
scope: The English (and historically Irish and Welsh) defence of the Church of England's establishment from the Victorian disestablishment campaigns to modern defenders such as Phillip Blond and Giles Coren, with Richard Hooker as the classic theorist. It is a single-issue stance, so most answers outside church and state are low-confidence inferences.

more-religion-public.rationale: Adherents value an established church that keeps a Christian presence in public institutions and ceremonies, though mostly as a settled arrangement rather than a campaign for more.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Defenders such as Blond and Coren present the established church as part of English national life and its rites.

gradual-change.rationale: Defending an inherited institution against abolition is a conservative, change-resisting stance that Hooker and later defenders frame as continuity.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Establishment rests on the monarch as Supreme Governor of the Church, so adherents treat the Crown as a legitimate head of state.

separate-church-state.rationale: The defining position is that the Church of England should stay established, with the monarch as Supreme Governor and bishops in the Lords, so strict separation is what adherents oppose.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Hooker grounds law in reason and tradition as well as scripture, and Church of England law is made by Parliament, not drawn directly from scripture.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Blond argues that the established church has blocked ethnic nationalism, implying a civic, inclusive national church.

total-state.rationale: Defenders credit the church with helping England resist totalitarianism (Blond).

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority rests on law and consent in Hooker, not personal oaths.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Same inference from Blond on racial nationalism;

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Adherents defend a church that runs thousands of state-funded schools, so they would not ban religious instruction there.

clerical-rule.rationale: Hooker held that King and Parliament, representing the whole commonwealth, govern the Church, and defenders keep bishops as one voice in Parliament, not its rulers.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: No stated position; Anglican parish tradition is rural but the stance makes no moral ranking of town and country.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: No stated position on national borders; adherents differ; This single-issue Church of England stance give no stated position on this, so it is left neutral.

death-penalty.rationale: No stated position; the Church of England has opposed capital punishment but defenders of establishment differ.

collective-defense.rationale: Nothing in the defence of establishment addresses alliances, so supporters are split.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Hooker has the King and Parliament represent the Church, but establishment's defenders do not call for curbing church property, so they are split.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax policy is outside this single-issue stance and supporters span the parties.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The established Church sits within the Crown-in-Parliament settlement, and Hooker has Parliament and King jointly represent the Church; Parliament is the sovereign legislator.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Establishment is about the church's engagement with public life, including bishops in the Lords, so withdrawal is contrary to its stance.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: The Church of England's teaching on marriage as a lifelong union led it to resist easy divorce, though it later accepted reform.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Antidisestablishmentarians defend King-in-Parliament as the constitutional settlement, which includes Parliament's control of supply.

residents-only-property.rationale: No stated position on local property restrictions; supporters differ.

non-intervention.rationale: Foreign policy is outside the stance; supporters differ.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The Church of England's establishment is not a case for criminal law, and modern defenders accept the present law; some traditionalists differ, so this is an inference.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Modern defenders argue that establishment gives access to the church's rites to everyone without penalising other faiths, and the blasphemy offence has been abolished in England; Hooker's tradition did tie church and commonwealth, so this is not a strong disagree.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Hooker and modern defenders support a constitutional establishment under the Crown in Parliament, which rejects armed removal of rulers; the establishment tradition works by law.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: A single-issue stance on church and state with no view on intersecting oppressions; supporters differ.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Defenders such as Blond and Coren come from different sides of politics; the doctrine has no view on the left-right divide.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Hooker's tradition grounds the commonwealth in laws of God while the Crown in Parliament remains the legal authority; the Church's establishment ties the state to a divine order, though modern defenders speak of national life rather than divine right.

social-market-economy.rationale: The doctrine is a single-issue stance and supporters range from free-market to social-democratic views.

rich-first.rationale: The doctrine has no position on development paths; supporters are split.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The doctrine has no foreign-policy position; supporters differ.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a constitutional or ceremonial crown, and the statement now asks only about passing real governing power to a child.

reviewHistory.rationale: Defenders of the established church back a hereditary monarchy, where the Crown passes by succession, but the doctrine concerns church and state and does not address this for leaders generally; adherents differ.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a constitutional or ceremonial crown, and the statement now asks only about passing real governing power to a child.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

reification.rationale: The doctrine has no stated position on reification; supporters are split.

racial-franchise.rationale: Defenders argue that establishment gives every English person access to the church and tempers nationalist extremism, which is incompatible with an ethnic franchise.

online-participation.rationale: Single-issue stance with no view on online participation; supporters differ.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Defenders argue that establishment tempers religious extremism and offers the church to everyone, so shunning a religious minority contradicts it.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: No stated position; supporters, like the Church of England itself, are divided.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Adherents split; Hooker's tradition sees church and commonwealth as one community, but the defence of establishment does not frame politics as a struggle of good and evil.

second-chamber.rationale: Defenders point to the Church's bishops sitting in the House of Lords, so a second chamber is part of the settlement they defend.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Defenders argue establishment keeps religion tied to the common life of the nation, which presumes a spiritual dimension that public life should serve.

language-defines-nation.rationale: A single-issue Church of England position; defenders hold varied views on nationhood.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Women's roles are contested among Anglicans; adherents are split.

capital-controls.rationale: Outside the doctrine; supporters hold varied economic views.

smash-state-machine.rationale: It defends the constitutional tie of church, Crown and Parliament and Hooker held that King and Parliament represent the Church, which is the opposite of smashing the state.

sacred-nation.rationale: Defenders hold that establishment ties religion to the common life of the nation, though they also argue it tempers nationalist extremism.

voter-id.rationale: Not a church-state issue; adherents are split.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Establishment gives the Church of England a legal tie to the Crown and Parliament that other churches and faiths lack, which defenders want kept.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Welfare design is outside the stance; adherents are split.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: The position does not address international justice and its defenders are split.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: The Church of England is a broad church that includes literalists and liberals, and defenders of establishment argue from national tradition rather than a doctrine of scripture.

national-church-status.rationale: This is the defining claim: the Church of England's legal ties to Crown and Parliament (Supreme Governor, bishops in the Lords) set it above other religious bodies, and defenders argue this should continue.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The stance is about church establishment; historically its defenders opposed disestablishment in Wales and Ireland, but nothing in it speaks to ethnic autonomy.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Establishment is a legal privilege for one denomination, the Church of England, so antidisestablishmentarians accept that the church has a public role in politics.

missingStatements.text: A country may properly have an official state church with a formal role in its constitution and national ceremonies.
missingStatements.rationale: This is the core claim of the defence of establishment, stated by the Church and by Blond and Coren.

notes: Advocates are split on other issues (for example same-sex marriage, where the Church of England itself is divided); those are scored 0. Some defenders, such as Hooker, rest the case on theology, others on pragmatic national benefits.
